title: When you break one
hook: the precepts are trainings, taken again and again; nobody keeps them perfectly

segments.voice: Yesterday, uposatha, the moon day with eight precepts. Your line was a day kept apart. Is the next full moon in your calendar? Day one hundred thirty, the end of the week of refuges and precepts.

Here's something that surprises people at a Buddhist temple. Someone who has been coming for forty years walks up to the monk and asks for the refuges and the five precepts. Again. They took them last week. They'll take them next week. Nobody thinks this is odd. Set that beside the usual voice after a broken promise: I blew it, so what's the point? One slip and the whole thing is over. Today, at the end of the precept week, a practical question: what happens when you break one?
screen: `FORTY YEARS, SAME PRECEPTS.` → `I BLEW IT, WHAT'S THE POINT?` → `WHEN YOU BREAK ONE.`

segments.voice: Remember the word at the end of every precept: samadiyami, I undertake. And the word before it: sikkhapada, a training step. Nobody undertakes a training they've already finished. The form of the precepts assumes you'll fall short, and that you'll take them up again. That's why people request them over and over. Each time is a fresh start, not a confession of failure. The Buddha gave his son Rahula a simple method for this, in the same talk as the dipper. Before you act, reflect: will this harm me or others? While acting, reflect again. And after acting, look back. If you find you did something harmful, don't hide it. Talk it over with a teacher or wise companions, and resolve to hold back next time. And if you look back and find no harm, he says, stay glad, and keep training day and night. There's no self-punishment in the list. Just honest looking, telling someone, and beginning again. The Dhammapada has a verse for the person who turns around. In Max Muller's translation: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." Tradition connects that verse with Angulimala, the bandit who became a monk. The verse doesn't pretend the clouds were never there. It says the moon comes out. So look back over the week. The three refuges: three places to rest. Not killing: let it live. Not taking: only what's given. Sexual conduct: no harm in love. Speech: say what's true. Pamada, and the moon day. Nobody keeps them perfectly. The training is to keep beginning again.
screen: `SAMADIYAMI: I UNDERTAKE, AGAIN.` · `LOOK BEFORE, DURING, AFTER.` · `TELL SOMEONE, THEN RESOLVE.` · `THE MOON FREED FROM CLOUDS.` · then, large: `BEGIN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Look back over the five precepts, slowly, one at a time: life, what's given, love, speech, pamada. Notice which one you slipped on this week, if any. No scolding. Just see it, the way Rahula was taught to look in the mirror. Then choose that one precept to take up again. If you'd like, say it inwardly in plain words: I undertake the training, again. Rest in the breath, like the moon coming out. The bell holds the time.
Samadiyami. I undertake: the word at the end of every precept, taken up again and again, however often you break one.
Your line: begin again. Today, recommit to one precept, the one you slipped on, and when you slip again, notice how quickly you can simply start over. Day one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Buddhists request the refuges and precepts again at temple visits and ceremonies; monastics confess faults to one another regularly, and lay people recommit simply by taking the precepts again.

fork.setup: you snapped at someone yesterday and said something untrue. you notice it today. what did the Buddha tell Rahula to do?
options: hide it and hope nobody noticed.
talk it over with someone wise, and resolve to do better.
give up the precepts: you're not cut out for them.
fork.reveal: look back, don't hide it, tell a teacher or wise friend, and resolve restraint next time. then keep training.

original.note: Pali: I undertake, I take up; the verb at the end of every precept, said again each time.

trapdoor: what you thought: break a precept and you've failed as a Buddhist.
what it means: the precepts are trainings, taken again and again; slipping is part of the path.
what a scholar hears: samadiyami is in the present tense, 'I undertake', and MN 61 gives a method of reflecting before, during and after every act.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 61 (Ambalatthika Rahulovada Sutta), reflecting before, during and after acting

sources.quoted: He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.

notes: Please check Max Muller's wording of Dhammapada 173 as quoted.
The tradition linking Dhammapada 173 with Angulimala (it appears in MN 86 as his verse) should be confirmed.

Rahula's method (reflect before, during, after; if harmful, confess to the Teacher or wise companions and resolve restraint; if harmless, abide in gladness and keep training) is paraphrased from MN 61.

Editor review 2026-10-01: SERIOUS fix: MN 61 says to abide in gladness when reflection finds an act was harmless, not after confessing a harmful one; teach, screen head and myth reveal corrected. Also cut 'most of us' and 'the most practical question of all', and replaced 'there's a moon behind yours' (telling the listener about themselves).
